title: THE FOUR HOMELESS TEENAGERS LEFT ME $1.45. WHAT I FOUND UNDER THAT NAPKIN THE NEXT MORNING CHANGED ALL OUR LIVES.
excerpt: At 2:17 in the morning, four teenagers walked into the diner where I worked.They were loud, exhausted, and clearly trying to pretend they weren’t worried about something.
author: admin

blocks.text: At 2:17 in the morning, four teenagers walked into the diner where I worked.They were loud, exhausted, and clearly trying to pretend they weren’t worried about something.
One wore a red hoodie with a torn sleeve. Another had a backpack with a broken zipper.
The third kept looking through the window every time headlights passed.

The fourth, a skinny boy with glasses, held a phone that looked like it had been dropped down a flight of stairs.They slid into the booth near the window.”Four waters,” the boy in the red hoodie announced.
I grabbed my notepad.”Anything else?”They looked at one another.”One basket of fries,” he finally said.
I stared at him.One basket of fries. Four teenagers. At nearly three in the morning.
I had been working the graveyard shift for eleven hours. My feet hurt, my back ached, and my landlord had left me two messages reminding me that rent was overdue.
I wasn’t in the mood for games.”That’s it?””Yes, ma’am.”I walked away, muttering under my breath.The diner was almost empty. An elderly truck driver sat at the counter nursing coffee.
A couple in work uniforms shared a plate of pancakes. The kitchen smelled like grease, coffee, and the cleaning chemicals we’d used on the floor.
I brought the teenagers their water and fries.
They immediately began dividing the fries into four little piles.

Not one of them took an extra.I noticed the boy in the red hoodie pushing two fries toward the youngest-looking girl.”Eat,” he whispered.”I’m not hungry.””You haven’t eaten since yesterday.”She looked down.
I pretended not to hear.I returned to the counter and started wiping it down.
That’s when their conversation reached me.
“I get paid Friday,” the boy with glasses said. “I can chip in for gas then.”
“Don’t worry about it,” another replied.
“How are we supposed to get there without gas?”
“I’m sleeping in the car tonight anyway. I don’t need gas.”
The boy in the red hoodie leaned forward.
He sounded like someone desperately trying to convince himself.
“I called three places today. Nobody has beds.”
“My mom said I could come home if I apologized.”
The dirty sneakers. The oversized jackets. The backpack with the broken zipper.
They weren’t teenagers hanging around after a party.
And that basket of fries was probably the only food they could afford.
Three cheeseburgers had been prepared incorrectly for another order. The customer had changed their mind, and the cook had already started making replacements.
They were sitting beneath the warming lights.
“Ray, what are you doing with those burgers?”
I grabbed the burgers, added cheese, lettuce, tomatoes, and extra fries. Then I made a large chocolate shake.
“Where are you going with that?” Ray asked.
The four teenagers immediately stopped talking.
“Wrong order. Three extra cheeseburgers and a shake. They’re going in the trash if nobody eats them.”
The boy with glasses looked at the burgers.
“Do I look like I have time to stand here arguing about hamburgers at two in the morning?”
I walked away before they could thank me.
For the next fifteen minutes, I pretended to be busy.
I watched them through the reflection in the coffee machine.
Not like teenagers enjoying a midnight snack.
Like people who hadn’t been certain when their next meal would come.
Lily wrapped half her burger in a napkin.
I had heard adults say that during hard times.
But hearing it from a girl who couldn’t have been older than sixteen was different.
When they finished, Marcus stood and approached the counter.
The four teenagers walked out into the cold night.
I watched them disappear beneath the streetlights.
There were crumbs everywhere, a few empty ketchup packets, and four glasses of water.
That’s when I noticed something underneath them.
They were already halfway across the parking lot.
They thought I might lose my job for feeding them.
I crouched slightly so I could look Marcus in the eyes.
“Listen to me. Nobody is getting in trouble tonight.”
“Buy yourselves something warm tomorrow.”
When I finally returned to the diner, I placed the $1.45 in my apron pocket.
Maybe I wasn’t ready to put it anywhere else.
I finished my shift at six in the morning.
On the drive home, I kept thinking about those four kids.
I wondered whether Lily would get to see her little brother.
I wondered whether Marcus had eaten anything before that basket of fries.
